title: Carry and Relative-Value Family: Harvesting the Roll, and the Convergence-Trade Blow-Up
content: Carry and relative-value (RV) strategies earn a structural premium by being short the same tails that trend-following is long: FX carry collects interest-rate differentials by staying long high-yielders and short low-yielders; bond roll-down harvests the term premium as securities slide down an upward-sloping curve; credit carry captures the spread between risky and risk-free coupons; equity-index futures basis and Treasury cash-futures basis trades exploit mechanical pricing gaps; vol carry (short variance swaps or strangles) monetizes the persistent gap between implied and realized volatility; and on-the-run/off-the-run swap-spread RV bets on the convergence of economically identical instruments. The strategy family earns steadily in regimes of positive carry, compressed spreads, ample funding, low realized volatility, and stable correlations — but all members share the same failure geometry: returns are negatively skewed and leverage-dependent, and the blow-up trigger is invariably a funding or liquidity shock that turns convergence into divergence. Canonical stress episodes are structurally identical: LTCM 1998 saw on-the-run/off-the-run spreads and swap spreads widen violently after Russia's default triggered a flight to liquidity, forcing margin calls that caused further widening in a self-reinforcing spiral at 25:1 gross leverage; August 2007's quant quake reflected crowded long-short equity RV books unwinding in lockstep after one large forced liquidation propagated through a shared factor, with risk models blind to tail correlation because the prior four years had been benign; and March 2020's Treasury basis trade unwind saw cash-futures spreads gap from roughly 20 bps to over 70 bps as repo rates surged and futures margin doubled, prompting hedge funds to sell an estimated $200 billion in cash Treasuries before Federal Reserve intervention stabilized the market. The conditioning variables that signal a hospitable carry regime — tight credit spreads, low VIX, steep funding curve, stable cross-asset correlations, and broad risk appetite — are precisely the variables that should trigger a crowding and fragility audit, because carry capacity is finite and excess positioning guarantees that any funding shock produces an exit far wider than the entry.
lesson: Carry and RV earn a liquidity-risk premium that looks like alpha in benign regimes but is structurally short a funding-shock tail; the blow-up signature is identical across episodes — crowded convergence positions meet a sudden liquidity event, divergence replaces convergence, and leverage amplifies the exit into a self-reinforcing unwind that requires external intervention to arrest.
